sources.title: Gill Fluke Treatment Guide: Dactylogyrus in Freshwater Fish
Efficacy of a therapeutic bath with selected antiparasitic drugs on a Dactylogyrus anchoratus infection in juvenile common carp (Cyprinus carpio)
CÁCH TRỊ BỆNH KÊNH MANG (SÁN LÁ) TRÊN CÁ KOI.

facts.fact: Gill flukes are monogeneans, small flatworms that live mostly outside the fish, on the skin, fins and gills.
Monogeneans have a direct life cycle: they pass straight from fish to fish with no intermediate host.
Dactylogyrids lay eggs and live mainly on the gills. They mostly infest freshwater cyprinids such as danios, barbs, goldfish and koi.
Gyrodactylids are mostly live-bearing, live mainly on the body and fins (sometimes the gills), and multiply fast in closed systems.
Dactylogyrids have two pairs of eye spots; gyrodactylids have none.
Adult flukes are typically about 600 µm long and flat and oval in shape.
In the wild these parasites seldom cause harm. In captivity, crowding can let parasite loads grow until fish sicken and die in large numbers.
Heavy gill infestations cause breathing problems; affected fish tolerate low oxygen poorly.
Heavy infestations can kill fish through secondary infections or loss of osmotic regulation.
At about 22–25°C, monogeneans can develop from egg to adult in only a few days. Near 1–2°C this can take five or six months.
Fast or laboured breathing, even when the water has enough oxygen.
Gill covers held flared open, or clamped shut.
Flashing (rubbing against the tank bottom, sides or decor).
Lethargy, swimming near the surface or crowding at filter outlets, and loss of appetite.
Severe cases: swollen, pale gills, faster breathing and gulping at the surface (piping).
Tiny dark spots may be visible on the gill filaments.
Skin flukes can cause scale loss and pinkish fluid at the attachment sites.
Clamped fins and skin discoloration where the parasites feed.
Confirming flukes needs a gill, fin or skin-mucus sample examined under a light microscope, from a live or freshly dead fish. The parasites decline quickly after the fish dies.
Work out which family is present, because treatment differs: egg-layers need longer treatment to kill the young as they hatch.
Look-alikes: bacterial gill disease and poor water quality. Test ammonia, nitrite and pH first.
Look-alike: gill irritation from chloramine in tap water that was not fully dechlorinated. Rule this out first.

Look-alike in koi: gill-cover flaring ('kênh mang') can be caused by cysts of larvae of the digenean fluke Centrocestus formosanus (spelled 'fomorsanus' on the page) deep in the gill filaments, not by monogeneans.
Flukes are often brought in on new fish that look healthy; carriers can infect fish that have never been exposed.
Stressors such as crowding, poor water quality, poor nutrition and aggression raise risk. The stress hormone cortisol has been shown to increase monogenean reproduction.
Eggs and larvae can survive off the fish in the tank.
Centrocestus larvae (the look-alike) reach fish via the snail Melanoides tuberculata. The adult worms live in birds and mammals, including humans.
Weak or heavily parasitised fish may not survive treatment.
Warm water holds less oxygen, so add aeration or surface agitation during treatment.
Remove fish from the treatment at once if they react badly.
Praziquantel is the treatment of choice for monogeneans. In the US it is not FDA-approved for fish, so a vet must prescribe it for this use.
Praziquantel bath: 2.5 mg/L for 24 hours, then a 50% water change. Repeat on day 7 and day 14 because it does not kill eggs.
Praziquantel in water at 2–3 mg/L: above 25°C treat every 3–4 days for 20 days in total; at 20–25°C every 4–5 days for 25 days in total.
To clear dactylogyrids from a closed system: three cycles of 5–6 days at 2.5 mg/L/day, with 1–4 medication-free weeks between cycles.
Praziquantel can also be given as a 10 mg/L bath for 3 hours, or at 35–125 mg/kg in food for up to 3 days.
Change 50–75% of the water between praziquantel treatments.
Long-term praziquantel: start at 2.5 mg/L and repeat every other day. Some species tolerated cumulative doses up to 10 mg/L.
Dissolve praziquantel powder in a small amount of alcohol, mix it into tank water in a bucket, then add it to the tank. Poorly dissolved powder can badly damage gills.
At therapeutic doses, praziquantel is described as safe for nearly all freshwater species, including shrimp, snails and live plants, and it does not harm the biological filter.
Kissing gouramis have reportedly reacted badly to Prazifish (a praziquantel product).
Formalin: 30 mg/L with vigorous aeration, re-treating after about 30 days if needed. Formalin uses up oxygen and sick fish tolerate it poorly.
Formalin 0.15–0.25 ml/L for 30–60 minutes, only in a well-aerated hospital tank. Never use it in display tanks with plants or invertebrates.
In juvenile common carp with Dactylogyrus anchoratus, a formaldehyde bath of 0.17 ml/l for 15 min and fenbendazole at 25 mg/l (2 × 12 h with a 24 h break) each cut infection by more than 90%.
The study's authors suggest registered fenbendazole products could replace unregistered formaldehyde for monogenean infections.
Also tested in that study: ivermectin 0.031 mg/l for 1 h, mebendazole 1 mg/l for 12 h, and levamisole 50 mg/l for 2 h or 3 × 1 h.
Levamisole at 2 mg/L is a second-line option with moderate effect.
Hydrogen peroxide 300–560 mg/L for 10 minutes. Use with extreme caution, as some fish cannot tolerate it.
Potassium permanganate: 2 mg/L as a long bath. Preferred when columnaris or water mould is also present.
Salt dip: 30–35 g/L for 3–5 minutes. For non-acute cases, a low-salt bath of 5 g/L for 90 minutes.
Seawater dip for freshwater fish: at least 10 minutes (15 for some monogeneans). Remove the fish if it rolls over.
Salt at 25 g/L for 15 minutes removed 100% of Gyrodactylus turnbulli but only 72% of G. bullatarudis, so salt results are unreliable.
Salt at 3–5 g/L gives mild relief but does not reliably kill adult flukes.
Organophosphates (trichlorfon, dichlorvos) were historically used at about 0.25 mg/L active ingredient. They are dangerous to fish and humans and banned for this use in many countries.
Trichlorfon at 0.5–2 ppm has been linked to spinal deformities in Melanotaenia pygmaea. Low oxygen makes organophosphates more toxic.
Dactycid can harm snails.
Some flukes have shown resistance to formaldehyde.
Before draining water from ornamental tanks treated with praziquantel, pass it through activated carbon.
Look-alike (Centrocestus): a koi seller reports that formalin, copper sulfate, salt, potassium permanganate and malachite green did not kill the larvae in the gills.

Look-alike (Centrocestus): the same seller gives praziquantel mixed into feed at 50–75 mg/kg of feed for 3–5 days, feeding 10–15% of body weight, and says this was tested at Vietnam National University of Agriculture.
Praziquantel smells strong: at high doses in feed, fish may refuse to eat, which reduces the effect. A binder helps keep the drug on the food.
Re-examine the fish under the microscope after treatment. The source's interval is garbled; it is likely 1–2 weeks.
Quarantine new fish for at least four weeks in a simple setup, with gill, fin and skin samples checked under a microscope.
Dip new fish before adding them to an established tank. Consider a preventive broad-spectrum parasite treatment during quarantine.
Fluke eggs are sticky and resist salinity changes, so a dip alone may not clear them.
Keep nutrition good and water quality stable to reduce stress.
Treat the tank as well as the fish, and repeat doses, because eggs and larvae survive off the host and eggs resist some treatments.
Flukes are very hard to eradicate otherwise, so empty, dry and disinfect tanks before restocking.
Skipping the follow-up praziquantel doses lets eggs hatch and restart the infection.
Using a conditioner that removes chlorine but not chloramine.
Overfeeding during treatment raises ammonia.
Adding new fish without quarantine.
Treating ponds with formalin at dusk; it uses up oxygen.
Reinfestation can occur 5–30 days after organophosphate treatment, so up to three treatments about 21 days apart may be needed.
Vietnamese koi keepers call gill-cover flaring 'kênh mang' and may call the disease 'sán lá'. One cause discussed there is Centrocestus larvae, not monogeneans.
A Vietnamese koi seller names densely stocked ponds and changing weather as high-risk conditions for heavy gill infections.
Rooms without air conditioning in tropical Singapore run 28–31°C; warm water holds less oxygen, so aerate well during treatment.
Salt is not a reliable way to kill adult flukes (Gensou).
Salt results are unreliable: in one study, raising salinity from 0 to 3 g/L increased gyrodactylid numbers (UF/IFAS article).
